results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which describes the mushroom body as divided into these three parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes; and the mushroom body lobe system, consisting of a vertical branch and a medial branch with different structures at different life stages. VFB holds various records related to the mushroom body, including neurons with some part in the mushroom body, parts of the mushroom body, and images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, with counts of [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body"), [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body"), and [22137](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in mushroom body") records, respectively.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response:
The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. This information comes from the VFB database, which describes antennal lobe projection neurons sending synaptic output to the mushroom body and lateral horn. VFB records show that these projection neurons generally send axons to higher brain centers, including the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. 

VFB holds various records related to the antennal lobe, including neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, neurons with synaptic terminals in the antennal lobe, and parts of the antennal lobe. However, for specific details on the brain regions connected to the antennal lobe, the VFB database summarizes region connections, indicating the connection to the mushroom body and lateral horn. 

To further explore the connectivity of the antennal lobe, you can examine the available data on neurons with presynaptic and postsynaptic terminals in the antennal lobe, as well as the tracts and nerves innervating the antennal lobe, which are all available in VFB.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain with specific characteristics and functions. According to VFB, it has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described by Klapoetke et al. (2017). This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4, as reported by Wu et al. (2016) and Tanaka and Clark (2022). Its arbors span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells, according to Wu et al. (2016). 

VFB records show that LPLC2 projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4, as described by Wu et al. (2016). The connectome data indicates that LPLC2 is connected to various neuron types, including sensory system neurons, visual system neurons, and projection neurons, with VFB finding 610 downstream class-connectivity partners for LPLC2. 

The activity of LPLC2 elicits a jump escape response, as reported by Wu et al. (2016) and Klapoetke et al. (2017). VFB holds data on approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe, as described by Wu et al. (2016), and they are cholinergic, according to Davis et al. (2020). 

For further information on the connectivity of LPLC2, you can query VFB for its downstream and upstream connectivity partners. VFB has annotated a range of data on LPLC2, including its neuron profile and connectivity partners, which can be accessed through the VFB interface.

results.title: Concepts: NBLAST
results.question: What is NBLAST and what does an NBLAST similarity score mean?
results.response:
NBLAST is a method to quantify morphological similarity, as documented in the Virtual Fly Brain documentation. According to this documentation, NBLAST works by finding the closest tangent vector in the target neuron for each tangent vector in the query neuron, with the final score being the sum over all query-target vector pairs, typically normalized to a self-self comparison with a perfect match being 1. This information is based on the documentation provided by Virtual Fly Brain, referencing the work of Costa et al., 2016. 

VFB does not currently hold data on the specific applications or interpretations of NBLAST similarity scores beyond this method description. To learn more about NBLAST and its uses, further queries can be made regarding its implementation and the datasets it has been applied to.

To explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons using Navis or pymaid, you can utilize these tools to analyze and visualize neuronal data. Navis is a Python package for working with neuronal morphology data, while pymaid is a Python interface to the CATMAID software, which is used for neural circuit reconstruction. 

The Virtual Fly Brain database holds various neuronal data, including neuron morphology and connectivity. You can use Navis to read and manipulate neuron morphology data from Virtual Fly Brain, and pymaid to access and analyze neuron data from CATMAID. 

However, the exact steps for exploring Virtual Fly Brain neurons using Navis or pymaid depend on the specific data and tools you are working with. You may need to consult the documentation for Navis and pymaid, as well as the Virtual Fly Brain database, to determine the best approach for your specific use case. 

VFB does not currently hold specific documentation or tutorials on using Navis or pymaid with Virtual Fly Brain data. You may need to refer to the documentation for these tools, or seek out additional resources or expertise, to learn more about how to use them together.

results.title: Anatomy teaching diagrams
results.question: Is there a circuit diagram of the mushroom body available on Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response: VFB holds various data related to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"), including neurons with some part in the mushroom body, neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body, and parts of the mushroom body. VFB also has images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body and expression patterns overlapping the mushroom body. However, VFB does not currently hold a specific circuit diagram of the mushroom body. The available data can be explored further to understand the structure and components of the mushroom body.
